title: A Sound of Thunder
full_review:
With all the stir currently surrounding the theory of evolution, the timing of Warner Bros.' release of "A Sound of Thunder" -- whose plot gimmick hinges on the topic -- couldn't be more ironic.

But there is one thing Darwinists, intelligent design proponents and creationists can all agree on: In the survival-of-the-fittest world of the box office, this movie will quickly go the way of the dodo.

Inspired by the classic short story of the same title by Ray Bradbury, this clumsy sci-fi action film, set in the near future, centers around a corporation -- Time Safari Inc. -- that offers carefully planned time-traveling excursions to wealthy thrill-seekers who pay top dollar to journey back to prehistoric times and hunt dinosaurs.

To insure against affecting the future, customers must obey three hard-and-fast rules: Don't change anything in the past, don't leave anything behind and don't bring anything back.

Badly miscast as brainy zoologist Travis Ryer -- the expedition leader -- is Edward Burns, who stars along with Ben Kingsley as the company's greedy CEO, Charles Hatton. Catherine McCormack plays Dr. Sonia Rand, who designed the time-traveling technology but whose Cassandra-like warnings about its inherent perils fall on deaf ears.
During one safari, a nervous hunter unknowingly kills a butterfly. The seemingly inconsequential misstep triggers a chain reaction of evolution-altering effects that end up rewriting millions of years of natural history and threaten to wipe out mankind in the process.

The team returns to a much different world, though at least initially the changes are subtle: unseasonably warm temperatures and odd behavior in sea life. But as more shock waves ripple from past to present, things get wilder. Killer plants take over downtown Chicago and a ferocious new species of predators -- half-lizard, half-baboon -- prowl the now-Amazon-like streets in hungry packs.

Together with Rand, Ryer must find a way to set things right before time catches up. Think "Jurassic Park" meets "Back to the Future."

Despite a tantalizingly intriguing concept, "A Sound of Thunder" turns Bradbury's masterfully economic yarn into a dud of an action flick, with a script as shaky as its science. Directed by Peter Hyams, the film doesn't even offer many B-movie thrills.

The visuals are wildly uneven. A "Jurassic Park"-flavored scene where the computer-generated raptor-apes stalk Ryer's team is quite scary, while other sequences resort to cheesy rear-projection techniques. It's as if the special-effects budget ran dry midstream.

In addition to characters dropping out of the narrative inexplicably and hokey contrivances, the film is riddled with brain-twisting illogic common to stories about tinkering with the time-space continuum.

And though "A Sound of Thunder" does impart a cautionary message about science overstepping its boundaries, you may end up wishing you could travel back in time and stop yourself from purchasing a ticket.

This film contains recurring sci-fi violence, including some intense scenes of menace, an implied sexual encounter with fleeting partial nudity, a suicide and scattered crude language and profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
